intro: Almost everything you will deploy runs on Linux: containers, Kubernetes nodes, CI runners, and most cloud servers. When a deployment fails at 2 a.m. there is no GUI, only a shell. This module gives you the working model of a Linux system that every later module assumes: where things live, who is allowed to touch them, what is running, and how to find out why it broke.
objectives: Navigate the filesystem and know what belongs in `/etc`, `/var`, `/usr`, `/home` and `/tmp`
Read and change file permissions and ownership, in both symbolic and octal form
Inspect, signal, and background processes, and manage long-running services with `systemctl`
Combine small tools with pipes and redirection to answer real questions about a system
Find the cause of a failing service from its logs using `journalctl`

sections.heading: The filesystem is a single tree

blocks.text: Linux has no drive letters. Everything hangs off one root directory, `/`, and extra disks, network shares, and even kernel information are **mounted** somewhere inside that tree. The layout is a convention called the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, and learning it means you can sit down at any server and know where to look.

rows: System-wide configuration, as plain text. The first place to look when behaviour is wrong.
Data that changes while the system runs: logs in `/var/log`, package caches, databases.
Installed programs and libraries (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`). Read-only in normal operation.
One directory per human user. `root`'s home is `/root`.
Scratch space, usually wiped on reboot. Never store anything you need here.
Not real files: a live view into the kernel and hardware.

blocks.text: Paths that start with `/` are **absolute**; anything else is **relative** to your current directory. Scripts and cron jobs should use absolute paths, because you cannot be sure which directory they start in.

blocks.code:
pwd                       # where am I?
ls -lah /var/log          # long listing, all files, human-readable sizes
cd /etc && ls | head      # move, then peek at the first ten entries
df -h                     # free space per mounted filesystem
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h | tail -5   # the five biggest things in /var/log

blocks.text: A full disk is one of the most common causes of mysterious outages. `df -h` to find the full filesystem, then `du -sh * | sort -h` to walk down to the culprit, is a routine worth memorising.

Every file has an owning **user**, an owning **group**, and three sets of permission bits: for the user, the group, and everyone else. Each set can grant **r**ead, **w**rite, and e**x**ecute. `ls -l` shows them as a ten-character string such as `-rwxr-x---`: a type flag, then three triplets.

The octal form is the same information as numbers: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1, and you add them up per triplet. So `rwx` is 7, `r-x` is 5, `r--` is 4, and `-rwxr-x---` is `750`. On a directory, execute means permission to enter it and read means permission to list it, which is why a directory with `r--` alone is nearly useless.

blocks.code:
ls -l deploy.sh                 # -rw-r--r-- 1 alice dev 412 Mar  3 10:12 deploy.sh
chmod u+x deploy.sh             # symbolic: add execute for the owning user
chmod 640 secrets.env           # octal: owner rw, group r, others nothing
chown alice:dev secrets.env     # change owner and group (needs root)
chmod -R g+rX /srv/app          # capital X: execute only on directories
id                              # which user am I, and which groups am I in?

blocks.text: The `root` user bypasses all of these checks, which is exactly why you should not work as root. Use `sudo` to run one command with elevated rights: it is logged, it can be limited per user, and it forces a moment of thought.

`chmod 777` makes a permission error disappear by letting every user on the machine modify the file. It is almost never the right fix. Work out which user the process runs as (`ps -o user= -p PID`) and grant that user, or its group, the minimum it needs.

A running program is a **process** with a numeric ID (PID), a parent, an owning user, and an exit code when it finishes. An exit code of `0` means success and anything else means failure. CI pipelines, shell `&&` chains, and Kubernetes probes all depend on that one convention.

blocks.code:
ps aux | head                   # every process, with owner, CPU and memory
ps -ef --forest | less          # the same, drawn as a parent/child tree
pgrep -a nginx                  # PIDs and command lines matching a name
top                             # live view; press q to quit (htop is friendlier)
ss -tulpn                       # which process is listening on which port
echo $?                         # exit code of the last command

blocks.text: You do not kill a process, you send it a **signal**. `SIGTERM` (15) is a polite request to shut down, and a well-written program catches it, finishes in-flight work, and exits. `SIGKILL` (9) cannot be caught: the kernel removes the process immediately, with no chance to flush data or release locks. Always try `SIGTERM` first.

blocks.code:
kill 4242            # SIGTERM by default
kill -9 4242         # SIGKILL: last resort only
kill -HUP 4242       # many daemons reload their config on SIGHUP
sleep 600 &          # trailing & runs a job in the background
jobs                 # list background jobs of this shell
fg %1                # bring job 1 back to the foreground

blocks.text: This matters directly for containers. When Kubernetes stops a pod it sends `SIGTERM`, waits for the grace period (30 seconds by default), then sends `SIGKILL`. An app that ignores `SIGTERM` drops requests on every deploy.

On nearly every modern distribution, long-running services are supervised by **systemd**. It starts them at boot in dependency order, restarts them when they crash, and captures their output. You talk to it with `systemctl`, and each service is described by a **unit file** ending in `.service`.

blocks.code:
systemctl status nginx          # running? since when? last log lines
sudo systemctl restart nginx    # stop, then start
sudo systemctl reload nginx     # re-read config without dropping connections
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx   # start at boot AND start right now
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=failed
systemctl cat nginx             # show the unit file that is actually in effect

blocks.text: `start` and `enable` are different things. `start` affects this moment; `enable` affects the next boot. A service that was started but never enabled works perfectly until the server reboots, a classic cause of an outage after routine patching.

blocks.caption: A minimal unit file: /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
blocks.code:
[Unit]
Description=My web app
After=network-online.target

[Service]
User=myapp
WorkingDirectory=/srv/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env
ExecStart=/srv/myapp/bin/server --port 8080
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

blocks.text: After creating or editing a unit file, run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` so systemd re-reads it. Note the `User=` line: the service runs as an unprivileged account, not as root.

sections.heading: Pipes, redirection, and the text toolkit

blocks.text: The Unix design idea is many small programs that each do one thing, connected by **pipes**. Every process has three standard streams: stdin (0), stdout (1), and stderr (2). The `|` operator connects one program's stdout to the next one's stdin; `>` and `>>` send a stream to a file.

blocks.code:
grep -ri "timeout" /etc/nginx/          # recursive, case-insensitive search
grep -c " 500 " access.log               # count matching lines
tail -f /var/log/syslog                  # follow a file as it grows

# top 5 client IPs in a web access log
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

./backup.sh > backup.log 2>&1            # stdout AND stderr into one file
./backup.sh 2> /dev/null                 # discard errors only
find /var/log -name "*.gz" -mtime +30    # files older than 30 days

blocks.text: Read that log pipeline left to right: take column one, sort so identical lines sit together, collapse them with a count, sort numerically in reverse, keep five. Nearly every investigation you do on a server is some variation of **filter, extract, count, sort**.
Order matters in `> file 2>&1`. It means: point stdout at the file, then point stderr at wherever stdout currently goes. Written the other way round, `2>&1 > file`, stderr still goes to the terminal.
systemd collects the output of every service in the **journal**. `journalctl` queries it, and its filters are what turn a wall of text into an answer.

blocks.code:
journalctl -u nginx --since "10 min ago"   # one service, recent window
journalctl -u nginx -f                      # follow live
journalctl -p err -b                        # errors and worse, since this boot
journalctl -k | tail -50                    # kernel messages (OOM kills show here)
dmesg -T | grep -i "out of memory"          # did the kernel kill something?

blocks.text: A reliable order of attack for "the service is down":

items: `systemctl status NAME`: is it running, failed, or restarting in a loop? Note the exit code.
`journalctl -u NAME --since "15 min ago"`: read the last lines before it stopped. The real error is usually the first one, not the last.
Check resources: `df -h` for disk, `free -h` for memory, `journalctl -k` for OOM kills.
Check the network: is it listening (`ss -tulpn`), and can you reach it locally (`curl -v localhost:8080`)?
Only then change something, one thing at a time, and watch the log while you do it.

practice.title: Run and break your own service
steps: Get a Linux shell you can safely damage: a cloud free-tier VM, or locally with `docker run -it --rm ubuntu bash` (for the systemd steps use a VM or Multipass).
Create a user `myapp` with `sudo useradd --system --create-home myapp`, and a directory `/srv/myapp` owned by it with mode `750`.
Write a unit file that runs `python3 -m http.server 8080` as `myapp` from `/srv/myapp`. Run `daemon-reload`, then `enable --now`, and prove it works with `curl localhost:8080`.
Find its PID with `pgrep`, send it `SIGKILL`, and watch systemd restart it. Find the restart in `journalctl -u myapp`.
Break it on purpose: change `User=` to a user that does not exist, restart, and diagnose it using only `systemctl status` and `journalctl`.
Write a one-line pipeline that lists the five largest files under `/var`, and another that counts how many processes each user is running.

focus: The filesystem map: config in `/etc`, changing data and logs in `/var`, programs in `/usr`.
Permission triplets and octal: r=4, w=2, x=1, so `750` is `rwxr-x---`. On directories, x means "may enter".
Exit code `0` is success, anything else is failure. All automation is built on this.
`systemctl start` is for now, `systemctl enable` is for the next boot. You usually want both.
Debugging order: status, then logs, then disk and memory, then network, then change one thing.

items.desc: Long listing including hidden files, human-readable sizes
Free space per filesystem
Size of each item here, smallest to largest
Files by name pattern, modified more than 7 days ago
Page through a file; `/text` searches, `q` quits
Follow a file as new lines arrive
Add execute for the owner (symbolic form)
Owner rw, group r, others none (octal form)
Change owner and group; add `-R` for a whole tree
Current user, UID, and group memberships
Run one command as another user
Every process with owner, CPU, memory
PIDs and command lines matching a name
Send `SIGTERM` (graceful)
Send `SIGKILL` (cannot be caught; last resort)
Listening TCP/UDP ports and the owning process
Exit code of the previous command
State, uptime, and last log lines
Start now and at every boot
Re-read unit files after editing them
Follow one service's logs
Logs for a time window
Errors and worse since the last boot
stdout of CMD1 becomes stdin of CMD2
Write stdout to FILE, replacing it (`>>` appends)
stdout and stderr both into FILE
Throw away error output
Count duplicates, most frequent first
Recursive, case-insensitive search

pitfalls: Fixing a permission error with `chmod 777` instead of finding out which user the process runs as.
Starting a service but never enabling it, so it silently stays down after the next reboot.
Reaching for `kill -9` first, which skips cleanup and can corrupt data or leave stale lock files.
Editing a unit file and forgetting `systemctl daemon-reload`, then wondering why nothing changed.
Using relative paths in scripts and cron jobs, which run from a directory you did not expect.

quiz.q: A file shows `-rw-r-----` in `ls -l`. Which octal mode is that?
quiz.explain: Owner `rw-` is 4+2=6, group `r--` is 4, others `---` is 0, giving 640.

quiz.q: You ran `sudo systemctl start myapp` and it works. After the server reboots for patching, the app is down. What is the most likely cause?
options: The service was never enabled, so it does not start at boot
The unit file was deleted by the reboot
systemd only restarts services that crashed, never after a reboot
The journal filled the disk during shutdown
quiz.explain: `start` only affects the current boot. `systemctl enable` (or `enable --now`) is what links the unit into the boot sequence.

quiz.q: Why should you send `SIGTERM` before resorting to `SIGKILL`?
options: `SIGTERM` can be caught, so the process can finish work and clean up before exiting
`SIGKILL` only works on processes owned by root
`SIGTERM` is faster because the kernel handles it directly
`SIGKILL` restarts the process instead of stopping it
quiz.explain: A program can handle `SIGTERM` to drain requests, flush data and release locks. `SIGKILL` is never delivered to the program at all; the kernel just removes it.

options: Writes both normal output and error output to out.log
Writes normal output to out.log and discards errors
Runs the job twice and logs the second run
Writes errors to out.log and normal output to the terminal
quiz.explain: `> out.log` points stdout at the file, then `2>&1` points stderr at the same place stdout is going.

quiz.q: A web service is reported down. Which is the best first step?
options: Run `systemctl status` on it, then read its recent `journalctl` output
Reboot the server so everything starts fresh
Send `kill -9` to every process owned by the app user
quiz.explain: Observe before you change anything. Status and logs tell you whether it crashed, is crash-looping, or is running but unreachable, and each of those has a different fix. Rebooting destroys the evidence.
